SELECT bm25(entries_fts, 2.0, 8.0, 4.0, 1.0, 1.0, 3.0) AS score,
       e.id, e.title, e.type, e.domain, e.subdomain, e.refutes,
       e.statement, e.true_theorem, e.hypothesis_violated,
       e.source_book, e.source_chapter, e.source_item, e.source_pages,
       e.difficulty, e.status, e.body_md, e.path
FROM entries_fts AS f
JOIN entries AS e ON e.id = f.id
WHERE entries_fts MATCH ?
ORDER BY score ASC, e.id COLLATE BINARY ASC
LIMIT ?

## Object

The verified witness, as recorded by the blind-search stage:

A two-type family population, all rational, no gender-responsive stopping rule, both boy-probabilities strictly interior:

  Type A: n = 2 children, boy-probability p_A = 3/4, population weight 1/2
  Type B: n = 3 children, boy-probability p_B = 1/2, population weight 1/2

Family size is a static attribute fixed in advance (children i.i.d. Bernoulli(p) given the type), so there is NO "family planning" / stopping rule reacting to realized sexes. The boy-probability IS heterogeneous across families (3/4 vs 1/2), so the claim's hypothesis holds.

Recomputed quantities (exact Fractions; K = boys, N = family size):
  E[K(K-1)]   = 1/2·2·1·(3/4)^2 + 1/2·3·2·(1/2)^2       = 21/16
  E[K]        = 1/2·2·(3/4) + 1/2·3·(1/2)               = 3/2
  E[#brothers | uniformly random MAN]   = (21/16)/(3/2) = 7/8   = 0.875
  E[K(N-K)]   = 1/2·2·1·(3/4)(1/4) + 1/2·3·2·(1/2)(1/2) = 15/16
  E[N-K]      = 1/2·2·(1/4) + 1/2·3·(1/2)               = 1
  E[#brothers | uniformly random WOMAN] = (15/16)/1     = 15/16 = 0.9375

So MAN (14/16) < WOMAN (15/16), deficit exactly 1/16 — the opposite of the asserted "men on average have more brothers". Both averages were independently re-derived by brute-force enumeration of all 2^n sex sequences of each family type with exact rational sequence probabilities, counting brothers person-by-person; the enumeration agrees exactly with the closed form (assertion in the script).

Also reported by the script: a still simpler degenerate witness ({n=1,p=1,w=1/2} + {n=2,p=1/2,w=1/2}: men 1/4 vs women 1/2) and a largest-gap witness ({n=1,p=1,w=7/8} + {n=6,p=7/8,w=1/8}: men 15/8 vs women 35/8). 1890 of the 9072 enumerated heterogeneous mixtures reverse the claimed inequality.

Mechanism: within one family type both a boy and a girl expect (n-1)p brothers; the population averages are the SAME numbers (n_i-1)p_i reweighted, by n_i·p_i·w_i for men versus n_i·(1-p_i)·w_i for women. Heterogeneity in p only guarantees the male tilt is toward high-p families; it gives men more brothers only if (n-1)p is increasing in p, which requires size to be uncorrelated with propensity. In the witness the low-p families are the LARGER ones, so (n-1)p is decreasing in p (3/4 for the p=3/4 type, 1 for the p=1/2 type) and the male size-bias points at the families with fewer brothers.

## What it kills

The flagged claim: **The answer's "in real life" conclusion (also its headline claim on line 0004) that heterogeneity of the boy-probability across families implies men have more brothers: "If the likelihood of having boys does depend on the family, men on average have more brothers, not fewer." This is asserted as a general implication of family-level heterogeneity in p, with only gender-responsive "family planning" excluded. It is false whenever family size is (statically) correlated with the family's boy-propensity, which heterogeneity alone does not preclude.**

The flawed step reads, verbatim from the source:

> If the likelihood of having boys does depend on the family, men on average have more brothers, not fewer.

Context of the original problem:

> Title: Do men or women have more brothers?
> 
> Do men or women have more brothers?
> 
> I think women have more as no man can be his own brother. But how one can prove it rigorously?
> 
> I am going to suggest some reasonable background assumptions:
> 
> There are a large number of individuals, of whom half are men and half are women.
> The individuals are partitioned into nonempty families.
> [...]

The witness satisfies every hypothesis the step assumes and falsifies its conclusion, refuting the step **as written**.

## Why it works

The verbatim sentence asserts a general implication: heterogeneity of the per-family boy-probability (with gender-responsive family planning explicitly excluded) implies E[#brothers | random man] > E[#brothers | random woman]. This is a finitely refutable statement — a witness is a finite family-type mixture with rational sizes, propensities and weights, and both conditional expectations are then rational and exactly computable as E[K(K-1)]/E[K] and E[K(N-K)]/E[N-K].

The claim is false as stated. Heterogeneity in p alone is not enough; one also needs family SIZE to be uninformative about the family's boy-propensity. The witness above satisfies every stated hypothesis (heterogeneous p, static family sizes, no stopping rule reacting to realized sexes) yet yields men 7/8 < women 15/16 brothers. Nothing in the claim's stated hypotheses precludes a static correlation between family size and boy-propensity, and such a correlation is not "family planning" in the sense the answer excludes — the number of children is fixed in advance and never reacts to which sexes actually appear.

Two exhaustive controls in the script confirm the diagnosis rather than a modelling slip:
  (C1) Homogeneous baseline: for all 42 single-type populations with 0<p<1 and n in 1..6, B_men == B_women EXACTLY, reproducing the classical "no difference" result the answer is arguing against.
  (C2) Equal-size control: over all 1512 two-type mixtures with n1 == n2 (size carries no information about p), there were ZERO violations of B_men >= B_women. So the answer's conclusion IS correct under the unstated extra hypothesis "family size uncorrelated with boy-propensity", and the flagged gap is precisely the omission of that hypothesis.
  (C3) Every reported witness's two averages were recomputed by direct person-by-person enumeration of all sex sequences and matched the closed form exactly (asserted, not merely printed).

All arithmetic is fractions.Fraction/int; no float is created anywhere and no decision is made from a float (decimals are printed only via an exact Fraction-to-string helper). The script is deterministic, stdlib-only, and runs in about 0.5 s.

- Verification: zero-import Lean 4 certificate vendored at `lean/canonical600/mse_1794123__ans1794617.lean` (kernel-checked in the source pipeline; certificate route None).

## Object

The max-times semiring on N — a close cousin of the tropical semiring — and its
polynomial extension. Leading coefficients no longer control products because
lower-order terms can absorb into the maximum.

## What it kills

The leading-term argument as an automatic inheritance principle. "Look at leading
coefficients" assumes the top-degree term of a product is the product of
top-degree terms, which uses additive cancellation twice.

## Debugging uses

- Tropical and max-plus polynomial algebra is the working context: factorization
  and root-counting intuition from classical polynomials fails at exactly this
  point, and this entry is the minimal demonstration.
- Completes the semiring suite (monic-not-regular, charp-zero-vs-charzero,
  direct-sum-complement-not-internal): each isolates one ring fact whose semiring
  failure traces to the same missing subtraction.
hits.counterexample: Let NatMaxAdd be the natural numbers with usual multiplication but maximum as addition: a commutative semiring that is a domain. Its polynomial semiring NatMaxAdd[X] is not a domain, even though NatMaxAdd has no zero-divisors other than 0; the classical proof breaks because addition is not cancellative (1 + 1 = 1 + 0 = 1).

## Object

The certificate witness, as recorded by the triage stage:

Triangle graph V={a,b,c}, E={ab,bc,ca}, with all edge weights 1. The cycle is a-b-c-a, and every edge is maximum-weight on it. Edge ab is maximum-weight, but T={ab,bc} is a spanning tree of total weight 2; every spanning tree has two unit-weight edges, so T is an MST and contains ab.

## What it kills

The flawed step of QEDBench problem Algorithms_18, solution 3, reads:

> Suppose G = (V, E) is a connected graph with weighted edges. Establish that for any cycle in G, the maximum-weight edge of that cycle is not included in the minimum spanning tree of G.

The witness satisfies every hypothesis the step assumes and falsifies its
conclusion, refuting the step **as written** (not necessarily the problem's
headline theorem — see the module docstring for scope).

## Why it works

From the Lean module docstring
(`lean/qedbench/ProofCerts/Algorithms/Alg18.lean`):

**Algorithms_18 (sol3) — a cycle's maximum-weight edge CAN lie in a minimum spanning tree**

The proof asserts the "cycle property" in a false, unconditional form:

> for any cycle in `G`, the maximum-weight edge of that cycle is not included in the
> minimum spanning tree of `G`.

The genuine cycle property requires the maximum-weight edge to be the **unique**
maximum; with ties it can fail. The asserted version drops that hypothesis.

**Counterexample — the unit-weight triangle.**
Vertices `V = {a, b, c}` (`a = 0`, `b = 1`, `c = 2`); edges `ab`, `bc`, `ca`, all of
weight `1`. The single cycle `a-b-c-a` uses all three edges, and since the weights
are tied every edge — in particular `ab` — is a maximum-weight edge of the cycle.

Every spanning tree of the triangle has exactly two edges (the three 2-edge subsets
`{ab,bc}`, `{bc,ca}`, `{ab,ca}` are precisely the spanning trees; the full 3-edge set
is the cycle, not a tree). Each has total weight `2`, so they are all minimum. Take
`T = {ab, bc}`: it is a minimum spanning tree and it **contains** `ab`, a maximum-weight
edge of the cycle. Hence the asserted claim fails.

**Modeling choices**
* Vertices `= Fin 3`; the three triangle edges are indexed by `Fin 3`
  (`0 = ab`, `1 = bc`, `2 = ca`), with `ends : Fin 3 → Fin 3 × Fin 3` giving endpoints
  and `w : Fin 3 → ℕ := fun _ => 1` the (uniform) weights.
* An edge subset is given as `S : Fin 3 → Bool` (membership). Its `weight` is the sum
  of `w e` over chosen edges; `numEdges` counts them. Because every weight is `1`,
  `weight S = numEdges S` definitionally.
* `Connects S` is a concrete, decidable predicate over `Fin 3`: starting from vertex
  `0`, the set of vertices reachable along chosen edges (three rounds suffice on three
  vertices) equals all of `{0,1,2}`.
* `IsSpanningTree S := Connects S ∧ numEdges S = 2` (a connected 2-edge subgraph on
  three vertices is exactly a spanning tree).
* `IsMST T := IsSpanningTree T ∧ ∀ S, IsSpanningTree S → weight T ≤ weight S`.
* "max-weight edge of the cycle" `IsCycleMaxEdge e := ∀ f, w f ≤ w e` (the cycle is all
  three edges; an edge is maximal on it when no edge is heavier).

**Decidability discipline (the GT7/Alg33 trap).** We NEVER ask `decide` to enumerate
the function type `Fin 3 → Bool`; that goes through `Fintype.piFinset` and gets stuck
in the kernel. Every `decide` here is over `Fin 3` / `Bool` (the kernel-robust regime)
applied to a *concrete* edge subset. The universally-quantified minimality fact
`∀ S, IsSpanningTree S → weight T ≤ weight S` is proved *algebraically*: since all
weights are `1`, `weight S = numEdges S`, and a spanning tree has `numEdges S = 2`, so
every spanning tree has weight exactly `2 = weight T`. No enumeration of subsets needed.

## Object

The verified witness, as recorded by the blind-search stage:

Circular-arc (indeed interval) graph on 4 vertices, given by an explicit arc model on a circle of 8 points: a = points {0,1}, b = {1,2}, c = {2}, d = {3,4,5,6,7,0}. Overlaps give exactly the edges a-b, b-c, a-d, i.e. the path c - b - a - d. Positive integer weights: w(a) = w(b) = 1, w(c) = w(d) = 2.

Independent sets and their weights: {} 0; {a} 1; {b} 1; {c} 2; {d} 2; {a,c} 3; {b,d} 3; {c,d} 4. Hence X = {c,d} is the UNIQUE maximum weight independent set, w(X) = 4 (next best 3), so "THE maximum weight independent set" is unambiguous.

Take Z = {a,b}. Z is a clique (a-b is an edge) and it is MAXIMAL (no other vertex is adjacent to both a and b: c is adjacent only to b, d only to a). Then X n Z = empty, so |X n Z| = 0, whereas the claim asserts |X n Z| = 1.

The case-0 sub-argument also fails explicitly on this witness: adding a to X breaks independence (a is adjacent to d in X), and adding b to X breaks independence (b is adjacent to c in X). So no vertex of Z can be added to X while preserving independence, and no contradiction with the maximality of w(X) is obtained.

## What it kills

The flagged claim: **The quoted Lemma 3: if X is a maximum weight independent set of a circular-arc graph A, then for any clique Z of A, |X ∩ Z| = 1 (in particular, the case-0 argument that if X ∩ Z = ∅ then some vertex of Z can be added to X while preserving independence).**

The flawed step reads, verbatim from the source:

> If $X$ is the maximum weight independent set of the circular-arc graph $A$, then for any clique $Z$ of $A$, we have that $\| X \cap Z\| = 1$.

Context of the original problem:

> Maximum Weight Independent Set in Circular-Arc Graphs (Proof of A Lemma)

The witness satisfies every hypothesis the step assumes and falsifies its conclusion, refuting the step **as written**.

## Why it works

The claim as stated is: for a circular-arc graph A with positive vertex weights and X a maximum weight independent set, every clique Z satisfies |X n Z| = 1. The inequality |X n Z| <= 1 is automatic (X independent, Z a clique), so the entire content is |X n Z| >= 1, i.e. that a maximum weight independent set must meet every clique. That is false, and the proof's "case 0" step is where it breaks: from X n Z = empty one cannot conclude that some vertex of Z is non-adjacent to all of X.

Witness: the path c - b - a - d (edges a-b, b-c, a-d), realised as an arc model on an 8-point circle (a = {0,1}, b = {1,2}, c = {2}, d = {3,4,5,6,7,0}), with weights w(a)=w(b)=1, w(c)=w(d)=2. The unique maximum weight independent set is X = {c,d} with w(X) = 4. The set Z = {a,b} is a maximal clique. Claim says |X n Z| = 1; here |X n Z| = 0. Moreover neither vertex of Z can be added to X (a is adjacent to d, b is adjacent to c), so the case-0 argument produces no larger independent set and no contradiction.

The script verified this exhaustively over its bounded space and found 216 such (weighted graph, X, Z) triples already at n = 4 vertices under the strict "Z is a maximal clique" reading, and 14705 more at n = 5; 3779 of the 14921 total have a unique maximum weight independent set. Note also that the failure is not specific to circular-arc graphs: the witness is already an interval graph. The correct statement is only |X n Z| <= 1.

        J2(v_a) = int_0^1 |v_a'| dt = |5/7 - 1| = 2/7

  v_b = ~v = (1, 1, 1, 1/2, 0)    [the answer's own recommendation: cruise at V, then brake at constant rate g = 2]
        int_0^1 v_b dt = 1/4*[1 + 1 + 3/4 + 1/4] = 3/4 = D             (feasible)
        J1(v_b) = 3/4
        J2(v_b) = 0 + 0 + 1/2 + 1/2 = 1

## What it kills

The flagged claim: **The answer asserts that minimizing total braking/acceleration effort, int_0^T |v'(t)| dt, is "equivalent" to maximizing the expected velocity at the green moment (i.e. that the two optimization problems have the same optimal strategies, namely any profile covering distance D by time T). This is false: the expected-velocity objective is maximized by EVERY feasible profile with int_0^T v = D, while int_0^T |v'| = V - v(T) strictly separates those profiles. In particular the answer's own recommended profile v-tilde (cruise at V, then brake at g) is the worst feasible profile for int|v'|, not a minimizer.**

The flawed step reads, verbatim from the source:

> is equivalent to what maximizing your expected velocity at the moment the light turns green, as was previously answered.

Context of the original problem:

> Title: Car, road, traffic-lights and an optimization problem.
> 
> Suppose you are driving on a road at speed $V$, and then at a distance
> $D$ you see a traffic lights showing "red". You are familiar with that
> road and know that the light will stay "red" for a time $T$, but as you
> just came around the corner you don't know how long it is already
> showing "red".
> 
> What is the best strategy to approach the traffic light, when you want
> your speed to be as high as possible$^1$ at the moment when the lights are
> [...]

The witness satisfies every hypothesis the step assumes and falsifies its conclusion, refuting the step **as written**.

## Why it works

The claim is that the two optimization problems "minimize int_0^T |v'|" and "maximize E[v(tau)] at the green moment" are equivalent, i.e. have the same optimal strategies, namely any profile covering D by time T. Refuting an equality of two argmin/argmax sets needs only a finite object: one feasible profile that lies in one optimal set and not the other. The script produces such a pair with exact rational arithmetic. Under the uniform green time implied by the referenced previous answer, E[v(tau)] = (1/T) int_0^T v = D/T is CONSTANT on the feasible set, so argmax J1 = F, the entire feasible set; but J2(v) = int|v'| = TotalVariation(v) is far from constant on F (25 distinct exact values in the N=4 sweep, 16 in the N=6 sweep), and equals V - v(T) on non-increasing profiles, so argmin J2 is the strict subset of profiles maximizing the terminal speed v(T). Since argmin J2 is a proper subset of argmax J1 = F, the problems are not equivalent, and any profile in F \ argmin J2 is a witness. The answer's own recommended ~v (cruise at V then brake at g) is such a witness and is in fact extremal in the wrong direction: cruising at V as long as possible front-loads the fixed area int v = D, which forces the smallest attainable terminal speed v(T) = 0 and hence the LARGEST braking effort V - v(T) = V among monotone feasible profiles, while the effort-minimizing strategy is a single early drop to the constant speed 5/7 (effort 2/7, a factor 7/2 less). The exhaustive search verifies all of this mechanically: J1 constant over every enumerated feasible profile, the identity int|v'| = V - v(T) on every monotone feasible profile, ~v attaining the monotone J2-maximum, and ~v strictly above the J2-minimum. All feasibility tests and all objective comparisons use Python int and fractions.Fraction only; no floating point enters any decision. Caveat on model fidelity (unavoidable in a blind run): the search reconstructs the feasible set from the claim's own description (initial/limit speed V, speed in [0,V], distance D covered by time T, uniform green time as in the referenced prior answer). If the original post imposed a further constraint that pins down v(T) exactly, the counterexample would need re-checking, but no such constraint is implied by the flagged sentence or by the recommended profile ~v, and the witness additionally survives an acceleration cap and a non-uniform green-time law.

## Object

WITNESS 1 — the EXISTENCE of the linear order ≿_p fails.
X = {a,b,c}, ≿ = {<a,a>,<a,b>,<b,a>,<b,b>,<c,c>}, i.e. a ~ b (mutual indifference, a ≠ b) and c incomparable to both. This is reflexive and transitive, hence a genuine preorder. Its incomparable ordered pairs are P = {<a,c>,<b,c>,<c,a>,<c,b>}, so P is NON-empty and the flagged sentence really is invoked here. Exhaustively checking all 3! = 6 linear orders on X (reflexive, transitive, antisymmetric, complete): the number extending ≿ is 0. Reason: any linear order ⊇ ≿ contains both <a,b> and <b,a>, and antisymmetry then forces a = b, contradiction. Claim says: for every p ∈ P a linear order ≿_p with ≿ ⊆ ≿_p and x ≿_p y exists; here the number of admissible ≿_p is 0 for 4 of the 4 pairs p ∈ P (0 out of 6 candidates each). Robustness: if "linear order" is read loosely as "complete preorder / weak order" (antisymmetry dropped), existence is rescued here (0 of 4 pairs fail), so this witness is specifically an antisymmetry failure.

WITNESS 2 — the INTERSECTION IDENTITY fails, for EVERY admissible choice.
X = {a,b}, ≿ = {<a,a>,<a,b>,<b,b>} (a strictly above b). ≿ is complete, so P = ∅ and the family {≿_p : p ∈ P} is empty; the intersection of an empty family of subsets of X² is X². Claim says intersection = ≿; here intersection = X² = {<a,a>,<a,b>,<b,a>,<b,b>} of size 4, while ≿ has size 3: |intersection| = 4 > |≿| = 3, the surplus pair being <b,a>, which is NOT in ≿ (indeed a ≻ b strictly). There is exactly one choice tuple (the empty one), so this was verified exhaustively, and it is independent of how "linear order" is read.

Sanity: at n = 3 the 12 cases are exactly the 13 weak orders on 3 elements minus the all-indifferent relation X², as expected.

## What it kills

The flagged claim: **In the final step that actually proves dim(X,≿) ≤ |X²|, the proof asserts that for every incomparable pair p = ⟨x,y⟩ one may take ≿_p to be a LINEAR ORDER on X extending ≿ with x ≿_p y, and that ≿ is the intersection of these ≿_p over p ∈ P. Both the existence of the ≿_p and the intersection identity fail on small explicit preorders: no linear order extends a preorder containing a nontrivial indifference pair, and when P = ∅ the empty intersection is X², not ≿.**

The flawed step reads, verbatim from the source:

> For each $p=\langle x,y\rangle\in P$ let $\succeq_p$ be a linear order on $X$ extending $\succeq$ and such that $x\succeq_p y$.

Context of the original problem:

> Title: Prove that $\dim(X,\succsim)\leq|X^2|$ - A starting point for a journey into order theory
> 
> During the last week I kept on thinking about what looked an easy problem at a first glance. 
> 
> Let $(X,\succsim)$ be a preordered set, and define $\mathcal{L}(\succsim)$ as the set of all complete preorders that extend $\succsim$. Define $\dim(X,\succsim)$ as the smallest positive integer $k$ such that $\succsim = R_1 \cap \cdots \cap R_k$ for some $R_i \in \mathcal{L}(\succsim)$, with $i=1,\cdots,k$.
> 
> Show that $\dim(X,\succsim)\leq|X^2|$.
> 
> In order to attack the problem, first of all I took a look at $\dim(X,X^2)$ and $\dim(X,\Delta_X)$, where $\Delta_X$ is the diagonal relation. In this question I got a feedback on my conclusions: indeed $\dim(X,X^2)=1$ and $\dim(X,\Delta_X)=2$. The interesting case is $\dim(X,\Delta_X)$, because this is the one that gave me a bit of intuition on how to a [...]

The witness satisfies every hypothesis the step assumes and falsifies its conclusion, refuting the step **as written**.

## Why it works

The flagged sentence asserts, for a preorder ≿ on X: (E) for each incomparable ordered pair p = <x,y> ∈ P there is a LINEAR order ≿_p on X with ≿ ⊆ ≿_p and x ≿_p y, and (I) ≿ = ∩_{p∈P} ≿_p. With "linear order" carrying its standard meaning (reflexive, transitive, antisymmetric, complete), both are refutable by a single finite preorder, and every quantifier involved ranges over finite sets, so an exhaustive small-|X| sweep decides them.

(E) fails whenever ≿ has a non-trivial indifference pair x ~ y (x ≠ y with both <x,y>,<y,x> ∈ ≿) together with at least one incomparable pair. A linear order extending ≿ must contain both <x,y> and <y,x>, and antisymmetry then gives x = y — so ZERO linear orders extend ≿ at all, and no ≿_p can be chosen for any p ∈ P. The script confirms this by enumerating all n! linear orders for each preorder: the minimal witness is X = {a,b,c} with a ~ b and c incomparable to both, where 0 of the 6 linear orders extend ≿ while |P| = 4. The proof therefore silently assumes ≿ is antisymmetric (a partial order); for a general preorder the step needs weak orders (complete preorders), not linear orders, and the search verifies that the loose "weak order" reading does rescue existence on this witness.

(I) fails whenever P = ∅ and ≿ ≠ X², i.e. whenever ≿ is complete but not the all-indifferent relation. The intersection of the empty family of subsets of X² is X², not ≿. The minimal witness is X = {a,b} with a ≻ b: the asserted identity would read {<a,a>,<a,b>,<b,b>} = {<a,a>,<a,b>,<b,a>,<b,b>}, false because <b,a> lies in the intersection but not in ≿ (size 4 vs 3). This is exhaustive over choices since the empty family admits exactly one choice.

Note on scope: these refute the quoted construction/step as written, not necessarily the headline inequality dim(X,≿) ≤ |X²|, which was not the target claim and was not tested. For preorders that ARE partial orders with P ≠ ∅ the intersection identity did hold for some choice in every case examined (0 failures under the "some choice" test), which is consistent with the classical Dushnik–Miller argument — so the defect is exactly the two degenerate regimes above: indifference (breaks existence) and completeness/P = ∅ (breaks the empty intersection).
